title: REAL BIBLICAL AUTHORITY KNOWS WHEN SCRIPTURE IS CLEAR—AND WHEN INTERPRETATION REQUIRES HUMILITY
paragraphs:
REAL BIBLICAL AUTHORITY KNOWS WHEN SCRIPTURE IS CLEAR—AND WHEN INTERPRETATION REQUIRES HUMILITY
The most dangerous Bible reader may not be the one who admits, “I don’t know.” It may be the one who never does.
There is a sentence some Christians are terrified to say.
“I could be wrong about this interpretation.”
Not wrong about Jesus being Lord.
Not uncertain about whether Christ rose from the dead.
Not embarrassed by Scripture.
Not surrendering biblical truth to whatever the culture wants truth to become.
Just humble enough to admit something every serious student of Scripture eventually discovers:
The Bible is infallible.
Our interpretation of every passage is not.
And confusing those two things can do terrible damage.
Because there is a strange kind of spiritual pride that can hold a Bible in its hands while quietly placing itself above correction.
It quotes verses.
It speaks confidently.
It knows theological vocabulary.
It may even say, “I’m just telling you what the Bible says.”
But sometimes what follows is not simply what the Bible says.
Sometimes it is what we believe the Bible means.
That distinction matters more than many of us realize.
You may have experienced the consequences personally.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to silence your questions.
Maybe you were told that disagreeing with one preacher meant disagreeing with God.
Maybe someone presented a disputed interpretation as though every faithful Christian for two thousand years had understood the passage exactly the same way.
Or perhaps this cuts closer.
Maybe you have done it too.
Maybe I have.
Maybe all of us who love Scripture need enough humility to ask whether we have ever attached God’s authority to conclusions God Himself did not state as explicitly as we claimed.
That question is uncomfortable.
Stay with it.
Because biblical authority is not strengthened when Christians pretend difficult passages are simple.
Biblical authority is honored when we refuse to make Scripture say either less or more than Scripture actually says.
Paul gave Timothy one of Christianity’s clearest declarations concerning Scripture:
“πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος…”
Pasa graphē theopneustos…
“All Scripture is God-breathed…”
That extraordinary word is θεόπνευστος — theopneustos, traditionally rendered “inspired by God” or “God-breathed.”
Paul continues by saying Scripture is profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, equipping the servant of God for every good work.
That is 2 Timothy 3:16–17.
Notice what Christianity confesses.
Scripture comes from God.
That does not mean every interpretation produced by a human reader comes from God.
Those are not the same claim.
The distinction is not modern skepticism.
Scripture itself gives us reasons for interpretive humility.
Peter said something remarkable about Paul’s letters.
He acknowledged that there were “some things in them that are hard to understand.”
The Greek expression includes:
δυσνόητά — dysnoēta
Things difficult to understand.
Peter did not conclude that because portions were difficult, Scripture was defective.
He warned instead that ignorant and unstable people twist those writings, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.
That is 2 Peter 3:15–16.
Think about the implications.
Scripture can be true while being difficult.
Scripture can be authoritative while requiring careful interpretation.
And a person can possess the text while distorting its meaning.
So saying, “This passage is difficult, and faithful Christians disagree about its precise interpretation,” is not necessarily weakness.
Sometimes it is intellectual honesty.
Sometimes it is spiritual maturity.
Sometimes the person most submitted to Scripture is the person willing to say:
“God has spoken clearly here.”
And somewhere else:
“I believe this interpretation is strongest, but I need humility because faithful Christians who honor Scripture have reached different conclusions.”
Real authority does not require pretending those sentences are identical.
Consider the Bereans.
Acts 17 tells us they received Paul’s message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether what they were hearing was true.
The Greek verb translated “examining” is associated with careful investigation:
ἀνακρίνοντες — anakrinontes
They investigated.
They examined.
They tested.
Imagine that.
Paul was preaching, and these people searched Scripture.
And Luke praises them for it.
Christian maturity therefore does not require switching off discernment when an impressive person opens a Bible.
Pastors should be tested by Scripture.
Teachers should be tested by Scripture.
Authors should be tested by Scripture.
Online ministries should be tested by Scripture.
Gospel Warrior should be tested by Scripture.
And this article should be tested by Scripture.
Because there is only one Christ.
Your favorite preacher is not Him.
Your denomination is not Him.
Your theological tradition is not Him.
And neither is the person writing these words.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
That should produce tremendous courage—and tremendous humility.
There are truths Scripture announces with breathtaking clarity.
God created.
Humanity sinned.
Sin separates and condemns.
God is holy.
Christ truly came in the flesh.
Jesus died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Salvation is found in Christ.
We are saved by grace through faith, not because our works placed God in our debt.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and faith.
Christ will return.
There will be resurrection and judgment.
Those truths are not embarrassing relics Christians need to soften until modern people approve of them.
The Gospel does not need our permission.
Jesus does not need cultural rehabilitation.
Where God has spoken clearly, humility does not mean becoming vague.
Sometimes humility means submitting even when obedience costs you.
But then there are questions where faithful Christians committed to biblical authority have disagreed over details of interpretation.
The precise chronology of end-times events.
The relationship between divine sovereignty and human responsibility.
Certain questions concerning spiritual gifts.
Particular questions of church government.
The interpretation of difficult prophetic imagery.
The meaning or application of individual passages whose linguistic, historical, literary, or canonical context requires careful work.
These issues matter.
Some matter enormously.
Humility is not saying doctrine does not matter.
Humility is refusing to pretend our confidence is greater than the evidence permits.
There is a difference between:
“Scripture says…”
and:
“My understanding of Scripture is…”
Mature believers learn when each sentence belongs.
And perhaps that is where this becomes personal.
Because certainty can become intoxicating.
It feels powerful to have an answer for everything.
It feels safe when the universe can be divided into people who agree with us and people who “reject Scripture.”
It feels reassuring to believe our theological tribe somehow escaped every blind spot that affected everyone else.
But pride has always been remarkably skilled at wearing religious clothing.
The Pharisee in Jesus’ parable was certain.
He prayed.
He fasted.
He tithed.
He compared himself favorably with somebody else.
Then, nearby, stood a tax collector who could barely lift his eyes.
His prayer was devastatingly simple:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
The Greek includes:
ὁ Θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ
Ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
And Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the other.
Luke 18:9–14 is not primarily a lesson about technical biblical interpretation.
It is something even more foundational.
It is a warning about the spiritual catastrophe of self-righteous certainty before God.
The Gospel begins by destroying our illusion that we are our own saviors.
And perhaps that same Gospel should destroy our illusion that we are incapable of misunderstanding anything.
The cross leaves no room for boasting.
At Calvary, nobody gets to stand above everybody else.
We kneel.
We repent.
We receive mercy.
We are corrected.
We are forgiven.
We learn.
We grow.
And when we discover we were wrong, Christians do not have to collapse.
Why?
Because our identity was never supposed to rest upon being right about everything.
It rests in Christ.
You can say, “I was wrong.”
You can say, “I misunderstood that passage.”
You can say, “I repeated something because my favorite teacher said it, but I never studied it carefully myself.”
You can apologize to somebody you wounded with your certainty.
You can reopen the Bible without fear.
Grace gives you permission to repent.
And repentance is not humiliation without hope.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a turning associated with a changed mind and direction.
Jesus did not come merely to make stubborn people more religious.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To reconcile.
To transform.
To make us His.
This is where biblical authority becomes beautiful rather than merely argumentative.
The goal of Scripture is not to give us ammunition for winning Facebook battles.
It leads us to know, trust, obey, proclaim, and worship the living God revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
Jesus told religious leaders who searched the Scriptures that those very Scriptures testified about Him, yet they refused to come to Him that they might have life.
You can study the map and still refuse the destination.
You can memorize verses and miss Christ.
You can win an argument and lose tenderness.
You can defend orthodoxy while feeding pride.
You can expose everybody else’s errors while hiding your own unrepentant heart.
And suddenly this article is no longer about “those Christians.”
It is about us.
About me.
About you.
What if the issue you desperately want to win is the very place where God wants to teach you humility?
What if somebody you dismissed has something you need to hear?
What if admitting uncertainty on a secondary matter would not weaken your faith but reveal that your faith is actually anchored somewhere stronger than your ego?
And what if, underneath all our arguments, there is an exhausted person reading this who does not need another theological performance?
Maybe you have been wounded by Christians who claimed divine authority for their own opinions.
Maybe someone made you feel that questions were rebellion.
Maybe you walked away from church because human arrogance was presented to you wearing God's name.
Please hear this carefully:
The failures of Christians do not make Jesus false.
Come back and look at Christ.
Not the caricature.
Not the manipulative leader.
Not the person who weaponized a verse.
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who received repentant sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrites.
The One who welcomed the broken.
The One who told the truth even when truth offended.
The One who went willingly to a cross.
The One who bore sin.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls:
Follow Me.
And maybe you are on the other side.
Maybe you are the one who has wounded people.
Maybe this exposed something.
Do not defend yourself too quickly.
There is grace here too.
Peter denied Christ and was restored.
Paul persecuted the church and became a herald of the Gospel.
Thomas doubted and eventually confessed Jesus as “My Lord and my God.”
Christianity is filled with people whose worst chapter did not become their final chapter.
That is our theme for a reason.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes pride and teaches surrender.
He takes shame and gives forgiveness.
He takes theological arrogance and produces teachability.
He takes sinners who were absolutely certain about themselves and brings them to the astonishing freedom of being absolutely dependent upon Him.
So study Scripture seriously.
Learn biblical languages if you are able.
Study history.
Understand literary genre.
Read Christians outside your immediate tradition.
Listen to faithful teachers.
Test everything.
Hold fast to what is good.
Know the difference between ancient words and modern assumptions.
Never use Greek or Hebrew merely to make an argument sound impressive.
The original languages are not decorative weapons.
They are languages God providentially used in giving us Scripture, and they deserve careful treatment.
And above everything, keep coming back to Jesus.
Biblical scholarship without Christ can become vanity.
Passion without truth can become deception.
Truth without love can become a weapon in sinful hands.
But truth received under the lordship of Jesus produces something different.
Conviction with compassion.
Courage with humility.
Doctrine with worship.
Authority without arrogance.
Faithfulness without pretending omniscience.
And perhaps one of the most spiritually mature sentences you will ever learn is this:
“Here I stand because Scripture is clear.”
Followed, when necessary, by another:
“Here is what I presently believe, but I may need correction.”
There is no shame in that second sentence.
The shame would be claiming God said something He did not say simply because our pride cannot tolerate uncertainty.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can itself be one practical way to steward what God has entrusted to you, while sharing these articles can help biblical truth reach people who may never enter a church building. Christ purchased our redemption. Grace cannot be bought.
Leave with Jesus.
Read His Word.
Test what you are taught.
Repent when Scripture confronts you.
Receive grace when you fail.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Speak boldly where God has spoken clearly.
Walk carefully where faithful interpretation requires humility.
And never confuse winning an argument about the Bible with surrendering your life to the Lord of the Bible.
Because one day, after our debates have gone silent and every platform has disappeared, it will not matter how impressive we sounded while defending our interpretations.
What will matter is whether the truth drove us to the feet of Christ.
The hands strong enough to hold tightly to truth should also be humble enough to open when Jesus shows us we were holding something that was never His.
